before: How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now? Try looking around the room, pausing before you act, making a choice and following through on it. If you can't do that because you're basically the frightened kid, leave the deeper conversation until later. You may need somebody steady there with you, or to do whatever helps you come back a bit before you try to talk to the child.
after:
## When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child

I've been writing this whole guide as if everybody who tries it wants to take care of the inner child. Some people get a little rush out of making somebody scared or small, though. For such folks, inner child therapy is clearly not the place to start. They need to first deconstruct the adult identity they've got.
guide_passage:
The r4 guide's passage (the passage this carries):
If you do want the relationship but a particular depth is too much, preserve the relationship by changing the dose. If you cannot reliably stop, return, stay oriented, or inward attention itself is making things worse, stop the inner exercise and come outward first. Do not test another inward technique just to prove you can tolerate something. Once you are steadier, the next gentlest step might be an ordinary protective action, real human support, or a brief eyes-open acknowledgment before imagery or deeper dialogue.

A complete tolerance pause is a last resort, and a safety problem can require a pause whether or not you want one. In that case, make the pause specific: what made it necessary, what level was last genuinely workable, and what observable change—plus your own agreement—would make a gentle return reasonable. While the pause is still active, do not keep testing gentler child-facing versions such as witnessing, imagery, or symbolic contact. Wait for the return condition instead. When you return, start at or below that last workable level rather than jumping back to where you left off. If a difficult experience still needs a check-in about how it landed or your system is still telling you to step down, settle that before trying to step back up. Changing the dose does not mean the relationship has failed, and this approach does not override your choice about whether to use inner-child framing at all.

Teaching points Joel approved (my wording, his yes on 2026-10-09 02:06), with what the article already says:
- T1: If a depth is too much, go gentler instead of pushing through with one technique after another, and instead of giving up on your little one. (Already in the article: "leave the deeper conversation until later" in the paragraph before; "I'd change course sooner (stopping counts)" in When to Change the Strategy. New: going shallower, and not hopping between techniques.)
- T2: If you can't stop and come back, or going inward is making it worse, come back out to the room first. Later, a gentle way back in is one protective thing in your life, or a short eyes-open hello before any imagery. ("real human support" is already the paragraph before's "somebody steady there with you".)
- T3: If you take a full break from your little one, note why and how far you'd got, and come back at or below that when you want to.
